A raw CBP message can be lost for good if an audit insert fails after an MQ get.
findings.recommendation:
Make the planned CbpTransmission / CbpInboundMessage tables the immutable system of record:
- Store byte-exact wireText/rawText with a sha256 hash, MQ MsgId, environment, filerCode, orgId, initiator (userId or apiKeyId plus IP) and timestamps.
- Add Postgres triggers that reject UPDATE of wire, hash or identity columns and any DELETE. Keep status changes in a separate append-only events table.
- Use onDelete: Restrict, never Cascade, on every CBP-record relation. Change Filing/AbiDocument/FilingStatusHistory/SubmissionLog org relations to Restrict and add a soft 'org closed' state.
- Persist inbound before ack (D2) inside a transaction that either succeeds or leaves the message on the queue. Never route CBP data through writeAuditLog.
- Make FilingDocument deletes soft and blocked once the filing is transmitted; keep the files under retention.
- Add a retention policy (records kept ≥ 5 years after entry or activity, plus a legal-hold flag) and an admin 'export records for filing/entry' bundle for CBP requests.
- Remove seed/reset scripts from the prod image.
findings.correction:
The cited facts are accurate: the cascades, the audit write that swallows failures (auditLog.ts:38-41), cert.received batches kept only as audit rows (certConsole.ts:362-373) with attach-logged replaying them, document hard-delete in any filing status (documents.ts:241-268), and the reaper resetting SENDING to DRAFT, after which the DRAFT can be deleted (abiDocuments.ts:244-259). Two corrections:
- The audit-only path is the platform-admin CERT console, which carries CBP CERT test traffic, not client PROD records. No native PROD transmission or inbound path exists yet, because abiGateway is still ccClient (services/abi/gateway.ts).
- No app route deletes an Organization or Filing, so the cascades are latent; they fire only on a manual or DB-level delete.
This is a must-design requirement for the Phase 1 inbound work, not a live data-loss path today. That makes it high, not critical.

findings.title: MFA bypass: chat, notification stream and staff-console stream accept the partial-auth mfaToken as a full session
findings.evidence: auth.ts:103-108 mfaToken = jwt.sign({ sub, typ: 'mfa' }, JWT_ACCESS_SECRET, 5m), handed out after password-only success (auth.ts:419-423). auth.ts middleware rejects typ (middleware/auth.ts:42-45) but chatAuth.ts:56 `jwt.verify(jwtCandidate, env.JWT_ACCESS_SECRET) as { sub: string }` has no typ check → actor kind 'user' with orgId; tools.ts:187-233 then returns the org's filings (BOLs, importer/consignee, rejection reasons). notifications.ts:32 and chatAdmin.ts:51 verify the same way. chatAdmin /stream then streams every org's chat conversations to anyone holding a platform admin's password.
findings.problem: Anyone holding only a password can read the organisation's filings through the assistant, and can subscribe to live notifications (BOLs, CBP transaction ids, rejection reasons). A platform admin's password alone exposes all cross-tenant chat traffic. They can also escalate to staff while showing as a verified user. MFA_PLAN.md required that any token carrying a 'typ' claim be rejected everywhere, but only authMiddleware does it.
findings.recommendation:
Create one verifyAccessToken() helper that:
- verifies the JWT and rejects any typ claim;
- loads the user and requires isActive.
Use it in authMiddleware, chatAuth, notifications /stream and chatAdmin /stream. Bind streams to the token's expiry, or re-check periodically and close them on deactivation. Add type-confusion tests for all four routes. Longer term, sign mfaTokens with a separate secret or audience.
findings.correction: Confirmed. chatAuth.ts:56, notifications.ts:32 and chatAdmin.ts:51 all call jwt.verify with JWT_ACCESS_SECRET and no typ check. The mfaToken (auth.ts:103-108) is signed with that same secret. Only middleware/auth.ts:42-45 rejects typ. The notifications /stream also never checks isActive.

findings.title: API keys skip the MFA/verified-email gate, never expire, survive member removal, and are invisible in the audit trail
findings.evidence: apiKeys.ts:39 `router.post('/', requireRole('owner', 'admin'), ...)`: no requireVerifiedEmail/requireMfaEnrolled and no writeAuditLog on create (:46) or revoke (:74). apiKeyAuth.ts:47-61 checks only keyHash/revokedAt; it never checks that createdBy is still active and there is no expiry. organization.ts:145-148 member removal sets isActive=false and refreshToken=null but leaves that member's keys live. publicApi.ts:91-98 and :134-145 submit ISF and send entries to CBP under actorUserId = key creator; filingWrite.ts passes no keyId/IP into writeAuditLog. The same gaps apply to webhook endpoint create/patch (webhooks.ts:51,84): no MFA gate and no audit row.
findings.problem: A newly provisioned owner or admin with mfaEnforced but not yet enrolled can mint an mcl_live_ key with a password alone, then transmit through the public API. That sidesteps the requireMfaEnrolled gate that protects UI submissions. A fired admin's key keeps filing under the client's filer code through Sigma's service-center queue. Afterwards nobody can tell a UI action from an API action, or which key did it.
findings.recommendation:
- Require requireVerifiedEmail + requireMfaEnrolled, and ideally a fresh step-up TOTP, to create keys and webhooks. Audit-log create, rotate and revoke.
- In apiKeyAuth, reject a key whose creator is inactive or whose org is suspended.
- Revoke a member's keys on removal or a downgrade below admin (or re-home them to a service principal).
- Add an optional expiresAt plus IP allowlist.
- Record apiKeyId and IP in the audit row and on CbpTransmission.
- Issue mcl_test_ prefixes on staging so CERT and PROD keys can't be confused.
findings.correction: Confirmed. apiKeys.ts:39 has requireRole only: no requireVerifiedEmail or requireMfaEnrolled, and no writeAuditLog on create or revoke. apiKeyAuth.ts:47-61 checks only keyHash and revokedAt. Member removal (organization.ts:145-148) and admin deactivation (admin.ts PATCH /users/:id) both leave the user's keys live. Webhook create and patch also have only requireRole.

findings.title: 'Viewer' role is not enforced: viewers can create, submit, amend, cancel and transmit to CBP, and change billing
findings.evidence: TeamPage.tsx:43 tells customers viewer = 'View-only access to filings'. requireRole appears only in apiKeys, compliance, organization, settings, tracking and webhooks; filings.ts (:409 submit, :420 amend, :564 cancel, :1211 bulk-submit), abiDocuments.ts (:493 send) and inbond.ts have no role gate. billing.ts:200 select-tier, :240 setup-intent, :263 card and :357 portal-session have no role gate, so any member can change the org's tier, replace the card or open the Stripe portal. documents.ts:241 lets any member delete documents.
findings.problem: With native transmission every submit is a CBP filing under the client's own filer code. A read-only seat that can file, amend or cancel ISFs and entries is a wrong-filing and liability risk. It also breaks a promise made in the product UI.
findings.recommendation:
- Define one permission map: VIEW, PREPARE (operator), TRANSMIT (operator+, optionally an org setting that limits it to admin), BILLING (owner/admin), ADMIN.
- Enforce it with requirePermission() on every mutating route, and keep it in sync with the shared services the public API uses (key scopes map to permissions).
- Add a route-matrix test that walks the router stack and fails if a mutating route has no permission guard.
findings.correction: Confirmed. requireRole is used only in apiKeys, compliance, organization, settings, tracking and webhooks. Submit, amend, cancel, bulk-submit, ABI send, inbond, documents and billing (select-tier, setup-intent, card, portal-session) have no role gate; some carry only the verified-email and MFA gates. The landing /security page (security-client.tsx:202) also promises 'Viewer: Read-only… Cannot edit anything.' The draw-entry-number endpoint is ungated too, so any member can burn entry numbers.

findings.title: Outbound transmissions are not exactly-once: no timeout, an unknown outcome is treated as 'not sent', and the reaper resets to DRAFT
findings.evidence: mqiptTransport.ts:44-49 `fetch(`${this.bridgeUrl}${path}`, { method, headers, body })` has no AbortSignal or timeout (undici waits up to ~300s). mq-bridge/index.js put uses MQPMO_NO_SYNCPOINT and returns MsgId only in the HTTP response, so a lost or timed-out response after a successful PUT leaves the outcome unknown. backgroundJobs.ts:445-451 rolls SENDING→DRAFT after 15 min with 'We deliberately don't try to reach CC for reconciliation' and clears sentAt; abiDocuments.ts:244-259 then allows deleting the DRAFT. publicApi POST /shipments and /entries take no Idempotency-Key.
findings.problem: When a send times out after CBP already queued the batch, the platform invites a resend: by the user, the reaper or an integrator retry. That means duplicate ISF adds, entry summaries or cargo releases at CBP, and the record of the first transmission gets erased. The spec covers inbound at-least-once (D2) but not outbound ambiguity.
findings.recommendation:
- In nativeTransmit, write CbpTransmission(QUEUED) before calling the bridge. Give it a 10–20s AbortSignal timeout.
- On timeout or network error, set SEND_UNKNOWN. Never auto-retry, and block user resend until reconciled.
- Reconcile using the B-record user-data tag echoed by CBP (D3), or the CBP response; give admins a manual 'confirmed not received' action with an audit row.
- Pass the transmission id as MQ CorrelId.
- Never return a transmitted document to DRAFT; drop the reaper for native.
- Accept an Idempotency-Key header on public API create/submit, stored per key for 24h.
findings.correction:
Confirmed: mqiptTransport.call (lines 44-49) uses fetch with no AbortSignal or timeout. The reaper (backgroundJobs.ts:445-451) rolls SENDING back to DRAFT and clears sentAt, a DRAFT can then be deleted, and the public API has no Idempotency-Key. Two corrections:
- The bridge put already accepts a correlationId and sets MQMD.CorrelId (mq-bridge/index.js:129-137), so the CorrelId plumbing exists.
- No native client transmission exists yet (abiGateway = ccClient). The outbound-ambiguity risk is therefore a Phase 1 design requirement, although the reaper has the same reset-after-possible-acceptance flaw on the CC path today.

findings.title: Outbound webhooks are effectively single-shot: about 1 second of retries, no event id, replayable signature
findings.evidence: webhooks.ts:9-11 'Delivery is best-effort: fire-and-forget... (A durable retry queue is a future enhancement)'; :29 MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3; :118 `await sleep(250 * attempt)`, so every retry finishes within about 0.75s. The payload (:58) `{ event, createdAt, data }` has no event/delivery id. The signature (:38-40) is HMAC(body) with no timestamp. emitWebhook (:63-67) runs in-process via `void dispatchWebhook(...)`, so a restart loses it. Emitted from notifications.ts:391/416/433 and abiPolling.ts:178.
findings.problem: Brokers integrating by API learn of CBP accept/reject only from these events. A receiver blip longer than a second, or a deploy, drops the 'filing.rejected' event for good, and an uncorrected ISF risks liquidated damages. Receivers can't dedupe the duplicates that timeouts already cause, and a captured delivery can be replayed indefinitely.
findings.recommendation:
- Add a WebhookDelivery outbox, written in the same transaction as the D5 verdict function: id, endpointId, event, payload, attempts, nextAttemptAt, status, lastStatus/lastError.
- Drain it with a worker using exponential backoff over at least 24h. Auto-disable an endpoint after N days of failures and notify the org admins.
- Add an `id` field and `MCL-Webhook-Id` header.
- Sign `t=<ts>,v1=HMAC(ts.body)` Stripe-style, and document a 5-minute tolerance.
- Expose a delivery log with 'resend' in the UI and API.
findings.correction: Confirmed: 3 attempts with 250ms and 500ms backoff, in-process fire-and-forget, a payload with no event id, and an HMAC over the body only with no timestamp. One detail: each attempt has an 8s timeout (DELIVERY_TIMEOUT_MS), so the total window is up to about 25s when the receiver hangs; it is under 1s only for fast failures such as 5xx or connection refused. No API integrators exist yet, so this must be fixed before the public API is sold, not before CERT.

findings.title: Webhook SSRF guard can be bypassed by redirects or DNS rebinding; mq-bridge auth fails open, exposing the destructive /receive
findings.evidence: webhooks.ts:81 runs assertPublicWebhookUrl (a separate DNS lookup, ssrfGuard.ts:112), then :97 `fetch(ep.url, { method: 'POST', ... })` with the default redirect: 'follow'. A tenant URL answering 307 → http://mq-bridge:8080/receive makes undici re-POST internally. mq-bridge/index.js:313 `if (CONFIG.token && req.headers['x-bridge-token'] !== CONFIG.token)` skips auth when the token is empty; compose passes `MQ_BRIDGE_TOKEN: ${MQIPT_BRIDGE_TOKEN:-}`. POST /receive does a destructive NO_SYNCPOINT get of up to 10 CBP messages. lastStatus/lastError are returned to the tenant (webhooks.ts:121-123, GET /webhooks), giving them an internal port-scan oracle.
findings.problem: Any client owner or admin can turn the webhook dispatcher into a proxy into the compose network. With an empty bridge token, which the server's new boot check prevents only for its own process and not for the bridge, that proxy can drain CBP responses for every client. More generally, the July SSRF fix (H1) can be bypassed.
findings.recommendation:
- Deliver with `redirect: 'manual'` and treat 3xx as failure.
- Pin the resolved IP: use an undici Agent with a custom lookup that re-validates each address with isBlockedIp at connect time.
- In the bridge, refuse to start without MQ_BRIDGE_TOKEN (fail closed, like envCheck.js), compare it with timingSafeEqual, and require it on /health as well.
- Optionally give the bridge its own compose network shared only with server.
findings.correction:
The SSRF bypass is real:
- deliverOne validates with a separate DNS lookup (ssrfGuard), then calls fetch with the default redirect: 'follow', so a 307 to an internal host or a DNS rebind gets through.
- lastStatus and lastError are returned to the tenant via GET /webhooks, which gives them a port-scan oracle.
The bridge-drain scenario is mostly mitigated:
- services/cbp/environment.ts:72-73 refuses to boot in production with ABI_TRANSPORT=mqipt and no MQIPT_BRIDGE_TOKEN.
- Compose feeds that same .env variable to the bridge (MQ_BRIDGE_TOKEN: ${MQIPT_BRIDGE_TOKEN:-}).
- A redirected webhook request never carries the x-bridge-token header.
A drain therefore needs a misconfiguration: the bridge profile running while the server is not on mqipt, or NODE_ENV not production. The bridge auth check at index.js:313 runs before routing, so /health is already protected whenever a token is set. Fail-closed startup and timingSafeEqual in the bridge are still worthwhile.

findings.title: Charge retries can double-charge, failed Stripe webhooks are never reprocessed, and admin plan changes clear delinquency
findings.evidence: billing.ts:72-81: on a retry, `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` returns no row and the handler returns 'duplicate event, ignoring'. The failure path (:100-104) only nulls processedAt, so a 500'd event is acknowledged 200 on Stripe's retry and never handled. retryFailedCharges is called concurrently from POST /billing/card (:307), the setup_intent.succeeded webhook (:133; its early-return at :120 only triggers if /card already wrote the pm) and the hourly cron. Each attempt uses `idempotencyKey: randomUUID()` (shipmentBilling.ts:142) on charges selected without a claim (:133-135). A crash between the 'pending' insert (:48-64) and chargeSavedCard leaves a 'pending' row that no sweep retries. admin.ts:193 `update: { planId: tier.id, status: 'active' }` silently clears 'delinquent'.
findings.problem: A customer saving a card can be charged twice for the same failed shipment. Payment-failure and refund webhooks that hit a transient error are lost, so delinquency and refund state drift away from Stripe.
findings.recommendation:
- Use processedAt for the webhook ledger: on conflict, re-run when processedAt IS NULL and receivedAt is older than a short window.
- Claim retries atomically: `updateMany({ where: { id, status: { in: [failed, requires_action] } }, data: { status: 'retrying' } })`, then use idempotencyKey = `${chargeId}:${attemptNo}`.
- Sweep 'pending' rows older than 15 min.
- Keep admin plan changes from overwriting 'delinquent'.
- Add tests for the concurrent /card + webhook path.
findings.correction:
Confirmed:
- handleStripeEvent returns 'duplicate' on any conflict, even when processedAt was nulled after a failure (billing.ts:72-81 and :100-104), so failed events are never reprocessed.
- retryFailedCharges selects charges without claiming them and uses randomUUID() as the idempotency key (shipmentBilling.ts:133-142). It can run concurrently from /card (:307), the setup_intent webhook (when the webhook lands before /card writes the payment method) and the cron.
- No sweep retries 'pending' rows.
- admin.ts:193 forces status 'active', which clears both 'delinquent' and 'card_on_file'.

findings.title: CBP connection credentials share a blast radius with the weaker staging VM
findings.evidence: Spec line 30: 'Keep the Middleware certificate; PROD = QGP2 ... | Same keystore on both VMs'. ci-cd.yml:12 and :292-297 auto-deploy any push to `staging` to the staging VM. The staging branch received two malware force-pushes (Sep 1, Sep 17; memory notes) using the owner's credentials, with rotation not confirmed. The staging VM also hosts the prod marketing site (deploy-landing uses the 'staging' environment, ci-cd.yml:554-560). compose:233-234 mounts /opt/mycargolens/mqipt read-only into the bridge; host file permissions are not codified.
findings.problem: Once PROD is live, compromising staging (the less protected box) yields a TLS identity accepted by CBP PROD's QGP2 channel. Combined with any leak of the PROD sender password, an attacker could transmit under client filer codes, or read and destroy CBP responses on Sigma's PROD outbound queue.
findings.recommendation:
Without reopening the hosting question, ask the CBP MQ team (MQSTAFFOPS) whether a separate certificate can be issued for CERT. If not:
- Require PR review and signed commits on staging (the branch already blocks force-push).
- Add a GitHub environment approval for staging deploys.
- Finish the incident #2 credential rotation.
- Store the keystore 0400, owned by the bridge uid, in a root-only directory; record its sha256.
- Keep the PROD sender password (D7) only on the prod VM.
- Alert on unexpected logins to the staging VM.
findings.correction: The facts are accurate: spec line 30 says 'Same keystore on both VMs', staging auto-deploys on push, and the keystore is mounted read-only from /opt/mycargolens/mqipt. This is an operational risk-reduction recommendation. CBP's own controls (source-IP allowlisting on the QGP2 channel, the separate PROD sender password) also limit what a stolen keystore alone can do, so medium fits better than high. The recommendation is sound and does not reopen the Contabo decision.

findings.title: Platform-level powers not bound to MFA; cross-tenant job triggers gated only by a client 'owner' role
findings.evidence: admin.ts:30-31 `router.use(authMiddleware); router.use(requirePlatformAdmin);`: no MFA check. The prod platform admin predates MFA and the schema defaults mfaEnforced to false (schema.prisma:104). index.ts:179-199 `/api/v1/jobs/status`, `/trigger-status-poll` and `/trigger-deadline-check` use `requireRole('owner')`, a CLIENT role, yet run global sweeps across every org (pollSubmittedFilings, checkDeadlines) and expose global job stats.
findings.problem: Phase 2 puts filer codes, service-center approvals and the per-org NATIVE/CC switch behind platform-admin routes, so a phished staff password could re-point filings. Separately, any client owner can trigger platform-wide polling and notification fan-out on demand.
findings.recommendation:
- requirePlatformAdmin must also require mfaEnabled (403 otherwise). Set mfaEnforced=true for all platform admins via a migration.
- Add TOTP step-up (re-verify within 5 min) for cbpConfig writes, gateway flips and service-center approvals.
- Move the /api/v1/jobs/* routes behind requirePlatformAdmin, or delete them.
- Add a stricter admin rate limiter.
findings.correction: Confirmed. admin.ts:30-31 and certConsole sit behind requirePlatformAdmin with no MFA check, and the schema defaults mfaEnforced to false. Only users provisioned after MFA get mfaEnforced=true (admin.ts:136, auth.ts:221). index.ts:179-199 exposes the jobs status and the global poll and deadline triggers to any client owner via requireRole('owner').

findings.title: Public /security page claims a hosting, backup and encryption posture that does not exist
findings.evidence: security-client.tsx:206 'Certificate pinning on critical API paths'; :207 'AES-256 disk encryption on the Postgres primary and all replicas. Backups encrypted with separate keys.'; :208 'Postgres + object storage hosted in AWS us-east-1 with backups to us-west-2'; :209 'Continuous WAL streaming + nightly full backups, 30-day retention. Quarterly restore drills documented.'; :214 'US (zero-retention API tier)'. Reality: a single Postgres container on a Contabo VPS (compose:22-31), local disk uploads, a local 14-day gzip backup script (BPR-01), no replicas, no WAL streaming, no drills.
findings.problem: These are false security and data-residency statements made to customs brokers on a compliance product, a regulatory and contractual liability. They also clash with the decision to stay on Contabo.
findings.recommendation: Rewrite the section so it states only what is true today. Ship the real controls (BPR-01, BPR-14) before the copy claims them. Add a CI grep guard for 'AWS', 'replica', 'WAL' and 'pinning' in landing copy, alongside the existing 'never claim a live CBP connection' rule.
findings.correction: Confirmed at security-client.tsx:206-209. The VENDORS table (:213-218) is also false: it lists 'AWS (us-east-1) Hosting + Postgres + S3' and 'Resend' for email, while the real setup is Contabo and Azure ACS SMTP. The ROLES copy promises a read-only Viewer that is not enforced (BPR-05).

findings.title: Deploy pipeline: mutable tags and tag-pinned actions, migrations that can brick rollback, hand-maintained CBP .env
findings.evidence:
Action and image pinning:
- ci-cd.yml:310 `appleboy/scp-action@v0.1.7`, :322 `appleboy/ssh-action@v1`, :169-197 docker/*@v3/v5/v6 are pinned by tag. The deploy job holds every prod secret (:330-371). The incident doc asked for 'pin/verify actions by SHA'.
- The docker job (:163-165, packages: write) runs `npm ci`/`npm run build`, where the malware executed. It can overwrite any existing SHA tag that prod later pulls: `.env IMAGE_TAG=<sha>` (:491), compose :57 `${IMAGE_TAG:-latest}`, and `:latest` is pushed from both branches (:182-184).

Migrations and rollback:
- docker-entrypoint.sh:10 `npx prisma migrate deploy` then `set -e`. A failed migration is recorded, so the rollback image's own `migrate deploy` hits P3009 and also crash-loops.
- The health-gated rollback (:513-519) only reverts the tag, and no pg_dump is taken first.

Hand-maintained .env:
- The new CBP variables (CBP_ENVIRONMENT, ABI_TRANSPORT, MQIPT_BRIDGE_TOKEN, COMPOSE_PROFILES, and later CBP_SENDER_*) are not in upsert_env (:449-474), so they exist only as hand edits on the VM.
findings.problem: The 219-commit promotion and the native go-live migrations (OrgCbpConfig, CbpTransmission, CbpInboundMessage) will apply to the prod DB automatically at container start, with no backup and no working rollback if a migration fails partway. The image-supply-chain guarantees are weaker than the SHA tags suggest. CBP-critical configuration has no record or check.
findings.recommendation:
- Pin every action to a commit SHA, with Dependabot for actions.
- Deploy by digest (record `docker buildx imagetools inspect` digests in .env). Stop pushing :latest from staging, or use per-branch tags.
- Run migrations as their own deploy step, `docker compose run --rm server npx prisma migrate deploy`, after `pg_dump -Fc` to the backup target, and fail the deploy before swapping images.
- Keep migrations expand/contract only.
- Add a committed .env manifest of names (no values), checked by a deploy step that fails when a required key is missing for the declared CBP_ENVIRONMENT.
- Log a values-free hash of the CBP section on each deploy.
- Extend the post-deploy gate to the bridge health and TRADE.VERIFY result (Phase 0.5) and the container SHA.
findings.correction:
Accurate:
- Actions are pinned by tag.
- :latest is pushed from both branches, and prod pulls by mutable tag, not digest.
- Migrations run in the entrypoint with no pre-deploy pg_dump, and rollback reverts only the tag.
- CBP variables are not in upsert_env.
Corrections:
- The deploy script already reads CBP_ENVIRONMENT and ABI_TRANSPORT from .env and refuses to deploy on a mismatch with the target (ci-cd.yml:391-402). The bridge is gated on its CBP environment too (:552+). So CBP config is checked; it just has no committed manifest.
- In docker-entrypoint.sh, set -e comes before prisma migrate deploy, not after. The effect is the same: a failed migration crash-loops the container.

findings.title: No CBP-grade observability: no metrics, alerts, request ids, or CBP-health signal; secrets leak into logs
findings.evidence:
Logging:
- index.ts:95 `morgan('combined')` logs full URLs, including `?token=<access JWT>` from notifications /stream, chat /events and chatAdmin /stream.
- No request id or pino-http, so a request can't be traced across pino and morgan lines.
- No `logging:` max-size in compose, so docker json logs are unbounded.

Error reporting and health:
- Sentry only captures Express errors and process nets (index.ts:226, :291-299). Job, billing and polling failures go to logger.error only.
- SPA Sentry can never activate: the Dockerfile:30-31 frontend stage declares only VITE_API_URL, and the CSP connectSrc (index.ts:74) has no Sentry ingest host.
- status.ts:22-43 publishes 'cbp.healthy' based on the CustomsCity poll cron.
- notificationDeliveryWorker.ts:163-174 parks emails as 'failed' after about 31 minutes with no alert.

External monitoring:
- TLS.md: the expiry watch is 'not yet active' until staging merges to main.
- Nothing monitors the MQ keystore expiry (~Aug 2027, memory).
findings.recommendation:
Logs:
- Add pino-http with a request id (propagated to bridge calls and stored on CbpTransmission).
- Redact the query token from logs (custom morgan token, or drop morgan).
- Set docker log rotation (max-size 50m, max-file 5).

Metrics and alerts:
- Expose an authenticated /metrics (prom-client) or push to Better Stack/Grafana Cloud. Track bridge_up{qmgr}, transmissions_pending_seconds (age of the oldest SENT without a response), inbound_unmatched_total, inbound_parse_errors, charge_failures, email_failed, webhook_failed and 5xx rate.
- Alert with on-call email/SMS on bridge down >5 min, the oldest unanswered ISF >30 min, any unmatched inbound, any permanent email failure for kinds filing_rejected or entry_rejected, and the MQ cert or public TLS expiring in <30 days.
- Send logger.error to Sentry through a pino transport.
- Re-base the public status strip on bridge health and inbound freshness.
findings.correction:
Confirmed:
- morgan('combined') at index.ts:95 logs the ?token= URLs.
- The Dockerfile declares only VITE_API_URL, so the main.tsx VITE_SENTRY_DSN is never set at build.
- The CSP connectSrc has no Sentry host.
- status.ts derives cbp.healthy from the CC status-poll cron.
- Compose sets no log rotation.
No metrics, alerting or request-id exist.

findings.title: PII and secrets stored in plaintext despite the schema claiming encryption; refresh tokens stored raw
findings.evidence: schema.prisma:16 `einNumber ... // Encrypted`, yet settings.ts:228 writes it raw and :248-257 copies the old and new EIN into audit_logs. IOR and consignee numbers (EIN or SSN-format for individuals) are raw in filings, abi_documents.payload and submission_logs.requestPayload. schema.prisma:92 refreshToken is stored raw, compared by equality (auth.ts:544) and written at :437-444. :611 the invite token is raw; :174 webhook secrets are raw. certConsole.ts:66-71 GET /params returns the whole row, including senderPassword, to the browser.
findings.problem: A DB dump or backup leak (backups are unencrypted gzip) exposes taxpayer identifiers. It also yields 7-day refresh tokens that can be replayed directly and pending invites that can be taken over. The schema comment misleads future developers.
findings.recommendation:
- Reuse the mfaCrypto AES-256-GCM helper with a DATA_ENC_KEY for EIN/IOR/SSN-like fields, plus a deterministic HMAC column for lookups.
- Mask them in audit values and logs.
- Store sha256(refreshToken) and the invite token hash.
- Encrypt webhook secrets.
- Never return senderPassword from the API (write-only field), and move it to .env per D7.
- Enable LUKS on the VPS volume if Contabo allows it, or at least encrypt backups.
findings.correction:
Confirmed:
- schema.prisma:16 claims '// Encrypted', but settings.ts writes einNumber raw.
- refreshToken (a signed JWT) is stored raw and compared by equality.
- certConsole GET /params returns senderPassword.
The senderPassword endpoint is reachable only by platform admins, and it holds a 6-character CERT sender password. Its exposure is limited, but it should still be write-only.

findings.title: Cron locking holds a 10-minute interactive transaction per job, and shutdown never drains jobs
findings.evidence:
Locking:
- distributedLock.ts:47-57 wraps each job in `prisma.$transaction(..., { timeout: 10 * 60 * 1000 })` around `pg_try_advisory_xact_lock`. The job body uses the global prisma client on other connections, so a pooled connection sits idle in the transaction for the whole run.
- On timeout the lock is released while fn() keeps running, so the next tick can overlap. Only status-poll, deadline and email jobs have in-process flags; charge retry, the ABI status poll and the reaper rely on the lock alone.
- Pool: connection_limit=20 (compose:78) shared by 8 jobs plus requests.

Shutdown:
- index.ts:260-276 never calls the exported waitForJobsToFinish (backgroundJobs.ts:599).
- server.close() waits on long-lived SSE sockets, so every stop ends in the 10s forced `process.exit(1)` and in-flight billing or polling work is cut off.
findings.problem: This is the wrong primitive for the Phase 1 inbound consumer (long bridge waits, persist then ack). Under load or during long outages it risks double processing and pool exhaustion, and deploys interrupt work mid-flight.
findings.recommendation:
- Use session-level pg_try_advisory_lock on a dedicated pg client (like the LISTEN clients), or a job_leases table with heartbeat and expiry, plus an AbortSignal passed into each job.
- Run the inbound consumer as one long-lived loop under such a lease.
- On SIGTERM: stop the crons, abort SSE streams (res.end), await waitForJobsToFinish plus the inbound loop's current batch, then disconnect.
- Set stop_grace_period: 30s in compose.
findings.correction:
Confirmed:
- withAdvisoryLock holds an interactive transaction with a 10-minute timeout around pg_try_advisory_xact_lock while fn uses the global client.
- The shutdown handler (index.ts:260-276) never awaits waitForJobsToFinish (backgroundJobs.ts:599) and force-exits after 10s.

findings.title: Rate limiting is double-counted on the public API and keyed per IP for multi-user broker offices; login lockout is an account-DoS
findings.evidence: index.ts:107 `app.use(generalLimiter)` applies globally. publicApi.ts:31 and status.ts:30 apply the same limiter instance again, so each request increments twice (express-rate-limit's singleCount only logs ERR_ERL_DOUBLE_COUNT after incrementing). The effective public API ceiling is 50 req/min per IP, despite the 300/min per-key limiter. The 100/min per-IP limit also covers the static SPA (served after the limiter, index.ts:209) and all users behind one office NAT. auth.ts:386-399 locks an account for 15 minutes after 5 wrong passwords from anyone, silently, including against the real user.
findings.problem: A broker ERP pushing a morning batch of ISFs, or a 10-person office polling notifications, will hit 429s. Anyone who knows a user's email can keep them locked out near an ISF deadline.
findings.recommendation:
- Apply the IP limiter once.
- Exempt static assets.
- Key authenticated traffic by userId or keyId with tier-based limits; keep IP limits for unauthenticated routes only.
- Replace the hard account lock with per-account+IP throttling and exponential delay, plus a CAPTCHA or email unlock link.
- Move to a Redis or Postgres store if more instances are added.
findings.correction: Confirmed. generalLimiter (100/min per IP) is mounted globally (index.ts:107) and again in publicApi.ts:31 and status.ts:30. In express-rate-limit 8.5.2, singleCount only validates after the store increment, so each request counts twice. A 5-attempt, 15-minute lock still applies to the real user (auth.ts:386-399); the code only hides the lock from the response.

findings.title: Boolean env kill-switches are broken: AI and chat can't be turned off with 'false'
findings.evidence: env.ts uses `AI_ASSESSMENT_ENABLED: z.coerce.boolean().default(false)`, `CHAT_ENABLED: z.coerce.boolean()` and `AI_DISABLE_TRAINING_DATA: z.coerce.boolean()`. Verified with the installed zod 3.25: `{A:'false'}` parses to true, and so does '0'. Compose passes `AI_ASSESSMENT_ENABLED: ${AI_ASSESSMENT_ENABLED:-false}`, the string 'false', so ai.ts:75 `env.AI_ASSESSMENT_ENABLED && env.AI_API_KEY.length > 0` enables AI whenever a key is present.
findings.problem: The operator can't stop customer trade data (filing contents) going to OpenAI, or disable chat in an incident, through configuration. That contradicts the stated privacy controls.
findings.recommendation: Use `z.enum(['true','false','1','0']).transform(v => v==='true'||v==='1')`, or z.stringbool in zod 4, for every flag, and unit-test the parsing. Audit the other coerce.boolean uses.
findings.correction: Verified locally: z.coerce.boolean().parse('false') returns true with zod ^3.25. This affects AI_ASSESSMENT_ENABLED (compose default 'false') and CHAT_ENABLED. AI_DISABLE_TRAINING_DATA also mis-parses, but it defaults to true, so the error is fail-safe there.

findings.title: No password reset path; 'Forgot password?' is a dead link
findings.evidence: LoginPage.tsx:266-268 renders 'Forgot password?' as a span with cursor-pointer and no handler. The server has no reset endpoint. admin.ts:212-238 resend-setup reaches only the org owner (`users: { where: { role: 'owner' ...}}`), so operators and admins have no recovery at all. auth.ts:762-794 set-password also doesn't reset lockout or failedAttempts.
findings.problem: A locked-out operator on an ISF deadline must reach Sigma staff, and staff can't help a non-owner. This is a support-load and production-readiness gap.
findings.correction:
Confirmed:
- LoginPage.tsx:266-268 renders an inert span.
- The server has no forgot or reset route.
- resend-setup targets only the org owner.
- Admin user routes offer only activate, deactivate and delete.
- set-password (auth.ts:779-782) does not clear failedAttempts, lockedUntil or refreshToken.

findings.title: Filer-mode and service-center data model needs authorization evidence and integrity constraints
findings.evidence: Spec D-table: ISF under S7P only when Sigma is the ISF filer, chosen per filing; OrgCbpConfig records only serviceCenterApprovedAt/By. schema.prisma:54-73 EntryNumberBlock has no CHECK (rangeStart ≤ rangeEnd ≤ 9999999, nextSequence bounds), no exclusion of overlapping ranges for the same filerCode across orgs, and nothing ties filerCode to the org's configured code. AbiDocument.entryNumber is globally @unique, so an overlap fails only at insert, after the number was drawn.
findings.problem: When Sigma files under S7P, Sigma carries the filer obligations. Each such filing needs evidence that the importer authorized Sigma (POA or written authorization), and the platform must block S7P mode for orgs without it. Overlapping or misconfigured entry-number blocks cause rejected entries and burned numbers.
findings.recommendation:
- Add OrgCbpConfig.sigmaFilerAuthorization: document id, signedAt, expiresAt, scope. Require it before any SIGMA-mode transmission.
- Store the client rep's approval email as an attached document.
- Add CHECK constraints and an exclusion constraint (btree_gist on filerCode + int4range) on EntryNumberBlock, and validate filerCode against OrgCbpConfig.filerCode.
- Record filerMode and filerCode on every CbpTransmission.
findings.correction:
The app-level Zod schema already enforces 1 ≤ rangeStart and rangeEnd ≤ 9,999,999 and rangeEnd ≥ rangeStart (settings.ts:320-327). Accurate:
- No DB CHECK or overlap-exclusion constraints exist.
- filerCode is free text that any org owner or admin can set (including S7P or another broker's code), with nothing tying it to an authorized org configuration.
- No authorization-evidence model exists for Sigma-as-filer.

findings.title: Realtime LISTEN reconnect is single-shot and SSE streams outlive token expiry or deactivation
findings.evidence: notificationStream.ts:71-80 reconnects once on 'error' via setTimeout. If that attempt fails, startNotificationStream's catch leaves isListening=false with no further retry, and 'end' isn't handled. chatStream.ts uses the same pattern. notifications.ts:23-67 checks the token only at connect time and never checks isActive.
findings.problem: After a Postgres restart longer than the delay, live updates stop until the process restarts (the UI falls back to 30s polling for notifications; chat breaks). A removed user's open tab keeps receiving events.
findings.recommendation:
- Retry with capped exponential backoff on both 'error' and 'end', and report listener state in health.
- Close streams at token expiry, and on deactivation via a pg_notify 'user_revoked'.
- If the inbound dispatcher uses LISTEN/NOTIFY, put it on the same hardened client.
findings.correction: Confirmed. notificationStream.ts reconnects once on 'error' via setTimeout. If the restart fails, the catch leaves isListening=false with no further retry, and 'end' is not handled. The SSE route checks only the token, at connect time.

findings.title: SMTP transport forces legacy SSLv3 cipher list and logs recipient PII on every send
findings.evidence: email.ts:59-63 `secure: false, ... tls: { ciphers: 'SSLv3', rejectUnauthorized: true }` (an old Outlook sample that restricts TLS 1.2 to legacy CBC-SHA suites). sendMail logs `{ to: options.to, subject }` at info for every message.
findings.problem: This weakens transport security for messages carrying filing statuses and OTP codes, and fills logs with personal email addresses.
findings.recommendation: Drop the ciphers override and set `minVersion: 'TLSv1.2'`. Log a hashed recipient or domain only, plus messageId.
findings.correction: Confirmed: email.ts sets tls.ciphers 'SSLv3', and every send logs `to` at info level (email.ts:131 and :134).

findings.title: ISF submit has no atomic claim: concurrent submits (double-click, API retry, UI + API, bulk-submit overlap) each transmit the filing
findings.evidence: filingWrite.ts:104-118 submitFilingToCBP reads the filing with findFirst and checks isValidTransition(filing.status, 'submitted') in memory. It then calls abiGateway.createDocument and, for ISF-10, abiGateway.sendDocument (:143-215). Only afterwards does it write the new status. Nothing like updateMany({where:{id, status:'draft'}, data:{status:'submitting'}}) claims the row first. ABI documents, by contrast, use a SENDING claim plus a reaper. The same function backs POST /filings/:id/submit, /bulk-submit and the public API POST /shipments/:id/submit.
findings.problem: Two requests that land within the CC/CBP round-trip both pass the status check and both transmit an ISF 'add'. Under native transmission this means duplicate ISF transactions at CBP for one shipment, followed by a rejection or a confusing second record. On the CC path it means duplicate CC documents. The billing anchor stops the double charge, but nothing stops the double filing.
findings.recommendation:
- Before any gateway call, atomically claim the filing: updateMany where status is in the submittable set, setting status 'submitting' and submittingAt = now(). Return 409 when count is 0.
- Resolve the claim to submitted or rejected in the same code path. Handle the unknown-outcome case like the outbound reconciliation in BPR-06 rather than resetting to draft.
- Add a concurrency test that fires two submits at once and asserts exactly one gateway call.

findings.title: User-fee tables stop at FY2026; FY2027 fees took effect 2026-10-01
findings.evidence: fees.ts:29-30 the newest MPF era is `{ from: '20251001', value: { minCents: 3358, maxCents: 65150 } }`. INFORMAL_FEE (fees.ts:107) `{ from: '20251001', value: 269 }`. MAIL_FEE (:121) and SURCHARGE (:135) also end at 20251001. pick() (fees.ts:16-21) returns the newest era for any later date. FR notice 2026-15530 (Jul 31 2026) sets FY2027 MPF min $34.58 / max $670.86 and informal $2.77, effective 2026-10-01. Today is 2026-10-15.
findings.problem: Since Oct 1, every entry the native path prices uses last year's fees: the MPF min/max clamp in applyMpfMinMax, the informal 311 fee, dutiable mail 496 and the manual surcharge 500. The duty estimate shown in the wizard (dutyEstimate.ts) and the shadow wire are already wrong. A native AE would report a 499 total that does not match ACE (rejection) or under-collects. Nothing alerts anyone when the table goes stale, and CBP adjusts these fees every October 1.
findings.recommendation: Add the FY2027 rows from FR 2026-15530: MPF 3458/67086, informal 277, plus the published mail and surcharge amounts. Add a unit test that fails when today is more than 12 months past the newest era. Add a startup or cron health check that warns admins from September 1 each year. Long term, keep the fee eras in a reference table maintained by admins, citing the FR document number.
findings.correction: Code facts are accurate: fees.ts MPF_LIMITS, INFORMAL_FEE, MAIL_FEE and SURCHARGE all end at the 20251001 era, and pick() returns that era for any later date. External facts check out: FR 2026-15530 (Jul 31 2026) sets the FY2027 MPF at $34.58 min / $670.86 max, effective Oct 1 2026. Downgraded from critical to high for three reasons. Native AE is not yet transmitting. ACE recomputes the 499 total and rejects a mismatch rather than accepting a wrong amount. The fix is a few table rows. What is wrong today: the wizard estimate (dutyEstimate.ts) and the shadow wire (abiShadow.ts) both use FY2026 limits.

findings.title: Foreign-currency invoice values are transmitted as US dollars
findings.evidence: migrateV1.ts:106 `valueDollars: Math.round(item.values.totalValueOfGoods)`. item.values.currency and exchangeRate are ignored. Invoice currency and rate are copied only into `commercial` (migrateV1.ts:204-205), which no mapper reads. The UI asks for the value 'In the item currency above.' (Step5Invoices.tsx:497) with an 'Item Currency' select and an 'Exchange Rate' field ('CC max: 8.'). Step6Review.tsx:177-179 multiplies value × item rate × invoice rate (a double conversion when both are set). There is no %R parser or rate store: '%R' appears only as a label in conditionCodes.ts:87. In cert, scenario 045 converted €5,000 to $5,796 by hand using CBP's %R rate (scenarios/index.ts:1617-1622).
findings.problem: A CNY ¥700,000 invoice goes on the 50-record as $700,000, and a JPY invoice can be overstated about 150×. EUR, GBP and CHF invoices are understated. The value drives duty, MPF, HMF and census data. Understatement is a 19 USC 1592 exposure, and ACE cannot detect it. 19 CFR 159.32-159.35 also require CBP's certified rate for the date of exportation, not a rate the user types in. The wrong values already appear in today's duty estimate and shadow wire.
findings.recommendation: Parse CBP's %R currency broadcasts, which already arrive on ACS.BRK.1303S7P.OUTBOUND, and keep them in a CbpCurrencyRate table (keep the FI/FR query as a fallback). Make migrateV1 convert each item with the certified rate for the invoice exportDate, using the quarterly rate unless the daily rate varies by 5% or more. Fail closed when the currency is not USD and no certified rate exists. Store the original amount, currency and the rate used for audit. Remove the user-entered exchange-rate field, or make it display-only.
findings.correction: Verified as stated. migrateV1.ts:106 takes item.values.totalValueOfGoods as dollars. Currency and exchangeRate are copied only into commercial.invoices, which no mapper reads. Step5Invoices.tsx:497 hints 'In the item currency above.' Step6Review.tsx:176-182 multiplies the item rate by the invoice rate. There is no %R parser or rate store; '%R' appears only at conditionCodes.ts:87. Scenario 045 (index.ts:1618-1622) converted the value by hand.

findings.title: Duty engine treats every ch.99 number as an additive overlay; in-lieu, replace and content rules exist only as hand-pinned cert values
findings.evidence: engine.ts:140-162: every 99xx tariff with value 0 computes its rate on the base value, and the base line keeps its own column-1 duty. The cert fixtures needed different semantics, pinned by hand. scenarios/index.ts:1018-1020: '9903.41.10 is an IN-LIEU rate, the 40% REPLACES column 1 ... (40% + 12.5% + 10% drew F624 live 9/1)', base `dutyCents: 0`. index.ts:231-240: 232 bucket `{ htsNumber: '99038210', valueDollars: 0, dutyCents: 2185230 }`, with the base at 0 and the NT52 number dropped when 9903.05.90 is present. Lines that are 232 derivatives also needed 54-record melt/pour or smelt/cast declarations (F794) and a 52-record steel license. The v1 payload collects `steelPercentage`/`aluminumPercentage`/`copperPercentage` (types.ts:106-108), but migrateV1 drops them. There is no logic to choose the required ch.99 numbers (F771 'fires until ALL are present') or their order (F852 HTS OUT OF SEQUENCE).
findings.problem: For real 2026 entries, which carry 301 + reciprocal + 232 + auto-parts stacks, the engine computes wrong line duty. 232 'bucket' and in-lieu lines get column 1 plus the surcharge. Content-value 232 duty is charged on the full value. Required declarations and licenses are missing. The result is F624/F771/F794/F852 rejections on most China and metal entries, and the wizard estimate shows clients the wrong landed cost. The cert pass hides this, because those duties were typed into the fixtures by hand.
findings.recommendation: Add a ch.99 semantics table keyed by heading range and effective dates: ADDITIVE (301, reciprocal), IN_LIEU (9903.41), REPLACES_COLUMN1 (232 buckets 9903.82/.94), CONTENT_VALUE (232 metal content, using the v1 percentages), EXEMPTION (rate 0, base unchanged). Turn the cert-proven ordering rules into a canonical sort. Have the engine return a 'missing required ch.99 / declaration / license' issue instead of guessing. Until this exists, fail closed: refuse native pricing for any line with a ch.99 number outside the table, and say so in the estimate.
findings.correction: engine.ts:140-162 prices every value-0 99xx tariff on the base value and leaves the base column-1 duty in place. The in-lieu (index.ts ~1014-1020), 232 bucket (index.ts 231-240) and GSP-lapse (index.ts 613-617) semantics exist only as hand-pinned dutyCents in the fixtures. migrateV1 drops steel/aluminum/copperPercentage. Nothing in the engine handles in-lieu, replacement or content-value rules. ACE recomputes and rejects mismatches (F624), so the main effect is rejections and wrong wizard estimates rather than silently accepted wrong duty. It still blocks native go-live for most China and metal entries.

findings.title: Rate source ignores entry dates, column 2 and lapsed programs, and specific rates are computed on whatever unit was reported
findings.evidence: dbRateSource.ts:26-27 `async getRate(htsNumber: string, _date?: string)`, which reads one current USITC edition, so ingesting a new edition rewrites rates for entries already in flight. The reader selects only generalRate/specialRate (dbRateSource.ts:15), although otherRate (column 2) is ingested (usitcHts.ts:84). Column 2 has applied to RU/BY since 2022, and engine.ts:118 always starts from `rate.general`. pickSpecialRate returns 'Free' for SPI A, but cert proved that GSP has lapsed and deposits at the general rate (scenarios/index.ts:613-617, 'Filing Free drew F624'). rateExpression.ts:119-123 says 'its UOM must be the unit the rate prescribes (the caller/refdata layer guarantees the pairing)', but nothing compares component.unit with uomCode1. migrateV1.ts:107 defaults the UOM to 'NO', and usitcHts `units` is never read. Commodity fees (cotton 056, sugar/dairy 110, and others, F657 in cert) are never computed. dutyEstimate.ts:89-92 and abiShadow.ts:39-40 use today's date in UTC as the applicability date.
findings.problem: A '4.4¢/kg' rate with quantity reported in NO (pieces), or a '/t' rate with quantity in KG, gives duty that is off by orders of magnitude. Goods from Russia or Belarus are priced at column 1. GSP claims deposit $0. Tariff changes with in-transit or date carve-outs are priced at today's rate instead of the entry's dates (ACE checks ch.99 numbers against the entry's own dates). Between 8 pm ET and midnight, UTC selects the next day's fee era and rates.
findings.recommendation: Make getRate date-aware and give it origin: store per-edition rows with begin/end dates, or better, cache CBP HA/HY results by as-of date (the HY parser already exposes beginEffectiveDate/endEffectiveDate, unitsOfMeasure, the duty formula code and tax/fee classes). Use column 2 for column-2 origins. Keep a lapsed-program table so the claim stays and the general rate is deposited. Reject a specific rate whose unit does not match the reported UOM, and default the UOM from the HTS units, never 'NO'. Compute commodity fees from the W5 tax/fee records. Derive the applicability date from the entry's legal date (arrival or entry, or withdrawal) in America/New_York.
findings.correction: One detail is overstated. dutyEstimate.ts uses the draft's dates.entryDate first and falls back to today in UTC only when that is absent (`options.applicabilityDate ?? parsed.data.dates.entryDate ?? todayYyyymmdd()`). abiShadow.ts always uses today in UTC. The rest is accurate. dbRateSource ignores the date and selects only generalRate/specialRate, although otherRate is ingested. computeDutyCents never checks the unit. The UOM defaults to 'NO'. Commodity fee classes (056, 110) exist only as labels in ae/tables.ts.

findings.title: Uncommitted multi-HTS mapper gives ch.99 overlays a UOM, unlike the cert-proven wire
findings.evidence: Uncommitted migrateV1.ts:114-120 sets `valueDollars: 0, // UOM is mandatory on every 50-record ... uomCode1: base.uomCode1` on each overlay. Yet every cert-accepted ch.99 row is `{ htsNumber: '99…', valueDollars: 0 }` with no UOM (scenarios/index.ts:91-92, 192-193, 1014-1016: 'CERT W1: 9903.41.10 has ZERO reporting units, omit uom/quantity entirely (the 9999.00.84 F441/F442 lesson)'). schemaV2.ts:40-42 made uomCode1 optional for exactly this reason. The overlay order is the user's input order (migrateV1.ts:111-122), while cert proved order rules (9999 marker first, 301 before NT52, 232 auto-parts last). multiHts.test.ts never asserts that overlays have no UOM.
findings.problem: Once committed, every multi-HTS line built natively would draw F441/F442-class rejections from ACE, plus F852 when the user enters overlays out of order. This is separate from the known /overlay-hts query bug.
findings.recommendation: Remove uomCode1 from overlay tariffs, and fix the stale comment in AeTariff. Sort ch.99 numbers into the CBP sequence before the base line. Add a golden test built from scenario 045 and 089 shapes: value 0, UOM and quantity blank, cert order.
findings.correction: The uncommitted diff adds `uomCode1: base.uomCode1` to every overlay. Every ch.99 row in the cert fixtures omits UOM, and schemaV2.ts:40-42 made uomCode1 optional for that reason (F441/F442). Overlay order is the user's input order. multiHts.test.ts never asserts that overlays have no UOM. Separately, the new abiDocument schema accepts any 8- or 10-digit number in additionalHtsNumbers, not only 99xx. A non-ch.99 'overlay' would get value 0 and become an unpriced tariff.

findings.title: Native ISF mapper fills in a US country, 'UNKNOWN' city and 'NA' street for parties with no address
findings.evidence: fromFiling.ts:374 `cleanAddress(...) || 'NA'`. :379 `|| 'UNKNOWN'; // legacy parity`. :384-385 `if (!countryRaw) { countryCode = 'US'; // legacy parity`. These apply to SE, BY, ST, LG, CS and every manufacturer (nameAddressBase is used at :597). This contradicts the header promise that 'the mapper never fabricates identifiers, names or origins' (:36-37). Also :413-418: when a manufacturer has no items, it is linked to every filing commodity. :571-572: the consignee silently falls back to the IOR EIN.
findings.problem: The seller, manufacturer, container stuffing location and consolidator are almost always foreign. A blank country becomes a US address with city UNKNOWN, transmitted under the filer's name (S7P or the client's code). CBP's edits do not catch this. It is inaccurate ISF data, open to ISF liquidated damages, and it degrades CBP targeting. Linking every manufacturer to every HTS line breaks the required ISF linkage between manufacturer, commodity and origin.
findings.recommendation: Remove the three fallbacks. Throw a field-level error on any party with no country, city or street line, with an ISF-specific message (for example 'Manufacturer 2: country is required'). Show the IOR-as-consignee fallback and the all-commodities linkage to the filer as warnings to confirm before transmit, never silently. Add tests for a party with no country.
findings.correction: The fallbacks are real: 'NA' street, 'UNKNOWN' city and country 'US' when no country is given, applied to SE/BY/ST/LG/CS and every manufacturer. Manufacturers with no items are linked to all commodities, and the consignee falls back to the IOR EIN. However, the code does not contradict an unqualified header promise. The header (fromFiling.ts:36-40) and nameAddressBase's doc comment explicitly list these as 'cosmetic legacy-parity' exceptions. The finding is that this carve-out is wrong for foreign parties, not that the code breaks its own contract. services/validation.ts treats a missing party country only as severity 'info', so nothing upstream blocks it.

findings.title: Native ISF misreports bill issuers, importer ID types and ISF-5 ports
findings.evidence: Bills: one SCAC is used for both the house bill (BM) and the master reference (fromFiling.ts:253-284, `bills: [{ qualifier: 'BM', scac, billNumber: house }]` and `MB ${scac}${master}`). The UI collects a single 'SCAC Code' with placeholder 'MAEU' (ShipmentWizard.tsx:1606-1608). billNumberOf strips only a prefix equal to that SCAC (:267). Importer IDs: normalizeEin (:227-234) forces every importer or consignee into EI form. An SSN '123-45-6789' becomes '12-345678900', and an 11-digit CBP-assigned number YYDDPP-NNNNN becomes '26-123456789', although IMPORTER_NUMBER_QUALIFIERS supports ANI and 34. ISF-5 ports: SF50 is always sent with the 'UN' qualifier (:556-559), but the UI stores 5-digit numeric codes from SCHEDULE_D_PORTS in foreignPortOfUnlading (ShipmentWizard.tsx:1943-1945), the same column that holds the 4-digit 'US Port of Arrival' on ISF-10 (:1618). placeOfDelivery is never collected in the wizard, so SF50 is never sent.
findings.problem: For house-bill (NVOCC) shipments, the ISF carries the ocean carrier's SCAC as the issuer, so it never matches the AMS house bill: no bill match, and the ISF counts as not on file (holds, liquidated damages). Non-resident or individual importers are filed under a fabricated EIN that identifies the wrong party or does not exist. ISF-5 filings carry an invalid port qualifier or no SF50.
findings.recommendation: Add a house-bill issuer SCAC per house bill (default it from the first 4 characters of the house bill when they form a valid SCAC, and confirm with the user). Detect the importer qualifier from the format (EI, ANI, 34, AEF) instead of forcing EI. Store ISF-5 ports in their own fields with an explicit K or UN qualifier and validate them against Schedule K or UN/LOCODE. Collect place of delivery.
findings.correction: Verified. buildBills uses one SCAC for both the BM house bill and the MB reference. normalizeEin turns a 9-digit SSN into 'NN-NNNNNNN00' and an 11-digit CBP-assigned number into EI form. ISF-5 SF50 is hard-coded to the 'UN' qualifier. The wizard stores 5-digit codes from SCHEDULE_D_PORTS in foreignPortOfUnlading; that list is mislabeled 'Schedule D' and holds CC's 5-digit values. The same column holds the 4-digit port on ISF-10. ShipmentWizard.tsx never collects placeOfDelivery, so the frob block (which needs both values) is never sent.

findings.title: Entry Type 86 is suspended at CBP, yet it is still on the native roadmap and in the product
findings.evidence: NATIVE_GO_LIVE_SPEC.md:40 'Type 86 cargo release follows once the SE path has passed CERT on staging.' cargoRelease/builder.ts:386 and :1029-1045 hold Type 86 rules, and recordDefs.ts:701 `'86': 'Section 321'`. CBP: ACE has rejected all Type 86 cargo release transmissions since 2025-08-29 (CSMS #66065494). CBP Dec. 26-12 (2026-06-24) suspended the Type 86 test, and FR 2026-12670 made the de minimis suspension indefinite for all modes except postal.
findings.problem: Work on native Type 86 would be wasted. Worse, the existing Type 86 product, built on CC in PR #117 per project memory, and any copy promoting it offer an entry type that CBP rejects. Low-value e-commerce shipments must now go as Type 11, or Type 01 above $2,500, with full duty and the informal fee, which is $2.77 for FY2027.
findings.recommendation: Remove Type 86 from spec scope item 5. Hide or flag Type 86 in the UI and the public API, with a clear notice. Make Type 11 informal (SE certify plus AE type 11, with header fee 311 from the corrected FY2027 table) the low-value path. Keep the SE Type 86 rules behind a disabled flag in case CBP reinstates the test.
findings.correction: CSMS #66065494 confirms ACE has rejected all Type 86 cargo release EDI since Aug 29 2025. The product side is worse than stated. src/data/abiEnums.ts lists '86 De Minimis (Type 86)' as enabled. Step1EntryShipment.tsx:93 says 'Consumption (01) and De Minimis / Type 86 are supported. Informal (11) is coming soon.' So today the wizard steers low-value shipments to the rejected type and gates the one that is required. Several landing pages (features, platform/filings, pricing, workflow, changelog) also mention de minimis / Type 86.

findings.title: MID derivation does not follow CBP's rules and is never checked with ACE
findings.evidence: mid.ts:118-122 uses the FIRST number on the address line (`party.address.toUpperCase().match(/\d+/)`). 19 CFR 102 App. and CBP Directive 3550-055 say to use 'the first four numbers in the largest number on the street address line' ('232 Main Street, Suite 1234' gives 1234). Common Asian address forms such as '3F, No. 1288 Zhongshan Rd' therefore give '3'. mid.ts:56-60 turns accented letters into word breaks: 'MÜLLER WERKZEUG' becomes the words M / LLER, so the MID reads MLLE… instead of MULWER. migrateV1.ts:61-75 sends the derived MID with no $I or MA check, although cert proved that 'MIDs must be pre-added via $I (F523 otherwise)' (certConsole.ts:418-420).
findings.problem: In PROD, a derived MID either does not exist in ACE (F523 MFGR CODE UNKNOWN, with no fix in the app) or collides with another firm's MID that is on file, so the entry names the wrong manufacturer. That is an accuracy problem for AD/CVD, textiles and targeting.
findings.recommendation: Use the largest number on the line. Transliterate before deriving (see ENG-10). In the filing flow, run $I Add Manufacturer, the builder for which already exists, for each manufacturer not yet verified. Store the MID ACE returns in an org-level manufacturer directory, and use only verified MIDs on native AEs.
findings.correction: Verified. mid.ts takes the first digit run (`match(/\d+/)`), not the largest number. nameWords replaces non-ASCII letters with spaces, so 'MÜLLER WERKZEUG' gives 'MLLE'. migrateV1 sends the derived MID with no $I verification; the $I builder exists only behind the cert console /transport/amf. The code comment cites 'Directive 3500-13'; the finding's 3550-055 citation is the current MID directive. Most failures are F523 rejections, plus a smaller risk of colliding with another firm's MID.

findings.title: Non-ASCII text either blocks a filing or is silently damaged, depending on the path
findings.evidence: codec.ts:116-136 upper-cases the value, then throws `value '…' violates class X` for any é, ü, ñ, curly quote or en-dash. AE descriptions and certify entities with such characters cannot be built, and the user sees a codec message. ISF cleanName (fromFiling.ts:186-193) deletes those characters ('SOCIÉTÉ GÉNÉRALE' becomes 'SOCIT GNRALE'). migrateV1.ts:84 `descriptions: [item.description.slice(0, 70)]` truncates descriptions, although schemaV2 allows several 44-records. The class X pattern allows '¢' (codec.ts:72), which is 2 bytes in the bridge's UTF-8 put (index.js:140) and breaks 80-byte framing when the delimiter is none.
findings.problem: Real supplier names and descriptions from Europe, Latin America, Turkey and Vietnam either block native AEs with an opaque message or reach CBP misspelled in ISF. Long descriptions are cut mid-word.
findings.recommendation: Write one shared toCatairText() for all builders: NFKD with combining marks stripped, ß to SS, Ø to O, smart quotes and dashes to ASCII, and drop '¢'. Return what it changed so the UI can show a warning. Split descriptions over 70 characters across multiple 44-records. Assert in the bridge that the message byte length equals the record count × 80 when the delimiter is none.
findings.correction: Verified. Codec class X rejects accented letters after upper-casing and allows '¢'. ISF cleanName deletes non-ASCII letters. migrateV1 truncates descriptions to 70 characters into a single 44-record.

findings.title: mq-bridge receive and connection handling lose messages and can stall the queue; delimiter default does not match the framing proven on CERT
findings.evidence:
These points are new beyond the known destructive cert-console drain.
- Error handling (index.js:158-161): `if (err) { if (err.mqrc === MQC.MQRC_NO_MSG_AVAILABLE) return resolve(null); return reject(err); }` under MQGMO_NO_SYNCPOINT|MQGMO_CONVERT. A warning such as 2119 NOT_CONVERTED arrives after the message is already removed, and is then rejected and discarded.
- Truncation (index.js:77): GET_BUFFER_BYTES=4MB without ACCEPT_TRUNCATED_MSG. An oversized message fails with 2080 and stays at the head of the queue, so every later poll fails.
- Shared connection: withSession (index.js:184-191) resets the single hConn shared by /send, /receive and /verify on any error, tearing down other in-flight calls. Under D2 syncpoint, MQCMIT and MQBACK are per hConn, so one ack would commit another request's gets.
- Event loop: GetSync is synchronous over the WAN and allocates 4MB every 500 ms poll.
- No timeout: mqiptTransport.ts:45 fetch has no AbortSignal.
- Framing: MQ_RECORD_DELIMITER defaults to 'lf' (index.js:59, compose :233, runbook 'default lf'), but staging's proven CBP framing is 'none' (project memory: 'mainframe 80-byte stream').
findings.problem: Inbound CBP verdicts can be lost silently, or one bad message can block all inbound traffic, the kind D2 is meant to prevent, unless the bridge is reworked rather than just given syncpoint. A prod VM that does not copy staging's .env override would send LF-framed batches to QGP2, a framing CERT never accepted.
findings.recommendation:
For D2:
- Use a dedicated receive hConn with MQGMO_SYNCPOINT and return MsgId and BackoutCount.
- Commit or back out only that hConn's unit of work, with a server-side ack deadline that backs out automatically.
- Treat MQCC_WARNING as success-with-flag, and persist the raw bytes plus CCSID.
- Use MQGMO_WAIT with a WaitInterval through the async Get instead of GetSync polling.
- Use ACCEPT_TRUNCATED_MSG plus a dead-letter path in our own DB for oversized messages.
- Use a separate send hConn, and fetch timeouts on the server.

Make 'none' the default in both index.js and compose, and update the runbook.
findings.correction: Verified. getOne rejects on any err other than 2033 under NO_SYNCPOINT; the ibmmq node binding raises err for MQCC_WARNING as well, so a removed message is lost. There is no ACCEPT_TRUNCATED_MSG. withSession resets the single shared hConn on any error. GetSync polls every 500 ms with a 4MB buffer. mqiptTransport fetch has no timeout. MQ_RECORD_DELIMITER defaults to 'lf' in index.js:59, compose :233 and runbook :68, while project memory records 'none' as the proven CBP framing. The 4MB truncation case is unlikely in practice, since CBP batches are tens of KB.

findings.title: Sends have no idempotency or 'unknown outcome' handling, so a retry can file twice with CBP
findings.evidence: mqiptTransport.ts:62-68: send() returns only after the bridge's HTTP reply. The bridge puts with MQPMO_NO_SYNCPOINT (index.js:139) and replies afterwards, so a crash, restart or socket drop between the MQPUT and the reply surfaces as 'mq-bridge unreachable' even though CBP has the batch. The spec's CbpTransmission statuses are 'QUEUED | SENT | ACCEPTED | REJECTED | CONDITIONAL | FAILED' (spec :111), with no unknown state. The cert console marks such failures as 502 and lets the user transmit again.
findings.problem: A user or job retrying a 'failed' ISF Add or AE Add sends it again. A duplicate ISF creates a second CBP ISF transaction that must be deleted. A duplicate AE Add for the same entry number may be rejected, but it confuses correlation, and a duplicate replace or delete may reach CBP twice.
findings.recommendation: Add SENDING and UNKNOWN states. Persist the wire text and a per-transmission tag (D3 user-data tag) before calling send. On any transport error after the request leaves, mark UNKNOWN, not FAILED. Resolve UNKNOWN by waiting for the tagged response through the dispatcher, or by an ISF/ES query, before allowing a retry. Never auto-retry an Add. Have the bridge accept a client-supplied idempotency key and reject a repeat key within 24 hours.
findings.correction: Verified. The bridge puts with MQPMO_NO_SYNCPOINT and replies afterwards. The spec's CbpTransmission statuses have no UNKNOWN state. In certConsole.ts the transmit handler leaves the row at status 'generated' on a transport error (transportErrorStatus returns 502). The same row can therefore be transmitted again even when the put reached CBP.

findings.title: Validators check structure but not reference data, date windows or ID formats, and CBP rejections reach users as raw codes
findings.evidence: validateEntrySummary checks codes only for entry type and MOT (entrySummary.ts:152-159). It does not check countries, Schedule D or K ports (F429, F167, F169 seen live), SPI against AE Table 8, UOM against HTS units, surety codes, state codes or fee class codes (USER_FEE_CLASS_CODES exists in ae/tables.ts:56 but is unused). Payment rules check weekends and holidays (:456-463) but not 'print date not in the past' (live F205 'SEP-1 TIME BOMB'). There is no check of exportation date against importation, and no IOR/EIN format check. Messages are spec-centric: `lines[0].parties[M]: mandatory for entry type 01 (ESF-134)`. CONDITION_CODES (conditionCodes.ts:6-50) covers only batch/block X-codes. AE F-codes, ISF SF90 codes and SX codes surface as 40-character CBP narratives. The cert-era meanings (F523, F624, F632, F657, F771, F794, F852, F441/F442, F205) live only in code comments and memory. ISF relies on builder throws, with no warnings for late filing (24 hours before lading).
findings.problem: Brokers get transmit-time rejections that the system could have caught, and cannot act on them. 'F771' or 'lines[0].parties[M]' means nothing to them, and spec success criterion 3 ('Rejections surface CBP's condition codes and narrative to the user') is met only literally.
findings.recommendation: Add a reference-data layer (ISO countries, Schedule D/K/UN-LOCODE, SPI table, surety list from the eBond download, HTS units from HA/HY), run in the validators as warnings or fatal issues. Add date-window rules evaluated in America/New_York. Build a CbpConditionCatalog (code, application, plain-English cause, suggested fix, and the UI field it maps to), seeded from the cert lessons, and map validator field paths to wizard field labels. Add ISF timeliness warnings.
findings.correction: Verified. The validator checks only entry type and MOT codes, plus the embargo list. USER_FEE_CLASS_CODES is only re-exported. The print-date check covers weekends and holidays but not past dates. CONDITION_CODES covers only batch-level X codes.

findings.title: No statement processing: brokers paying by ACH statement cannot reconcile or authorize payment in the platform
findings.evidence: The validator and migrateV1 accept payment types 2/3/5/6/7/8 with a preliminary statement print date (entrySummary.ts:431-482; migrateV1.ts:138-163). Statement apps exist only as labels: dailyStatement 'PF', periodicMonthlyStatement 'MS', statementUpdate SU/SQ, achDebitAuthorization RM/PZ (conditionCodes.ts:72-82). There is no PF/MS parser and no RM builder. On the positive side, OUTPUT_B already parses the statement fields (recordDefs.ts:133-138). The spec puts statement parsing out of scope (spec :44).
findings.problem: Statement payment is how most brokers pay CBP. Natively they could file statement-paid entries but never see the preliminary or final statement, the statement number, or totals. They could not transmit the ACH debit authorization or move an entry between statements, so payment would have to be done outside the platform. A missed authorization means late-payment interest and can cost the importer its statement privileges. That makes the native offer weaker than CC-era expectations for broker clients.
findings.recommendation: Plan a phase right after go-live: a PF/MS parser over the persisted CbpInboundMessage rows, a statement ledger UI that reconciles each entry against its statement, the RM ACH debit authorization with a two-person approval, and SU statement update. Until then, document clearly that payment type 1 or out-of-band payment is required, and warn when type 2 or 6 is selected.
findings.correction: Statement applications exist only as labels in conditionCodes.ts. The spec explicitly puts statement parsing out of scope. migrateV1 accepts payment types 2/3/5/6/7/8.

findings.title: Duty enrichment keeps any existing per-tariff duty, so an edited payload keeps old amounts
findings.evidence: engine.ts:74-78 'existing tariff duty amounts are kept, fees and totals are always recomputed'. engine.ts:109 computes only `if (tariff.dutyCents === undefined)`. schemaV2.ts:37 says 'Absent = not yet computed (duty engine fills it)', and the plan stores v2 as JSONB on AbiDocument.
findings.problem: Once v2 payloads are stored natively, which is the plan, an enriched payload whose value, quantity, origin or SPI is later edited keeps the old line duty. Fees and grand totals are recomputed around it, so the summary looks consistent but under- or over-declares duty. Today the v1→v2 path rebuilds from scratch on every call, which hides the problem.
findings.recommendation: Separate 'duty supplied by the filer' from 'duty computed by the engine': store dutySource on each tariff. Always recompute engine-sourced duty on enrichment, and require explicit confirmation for filer overrides. Add a test that edits the value and re-enriches.
findings.correction: engine.ts:109 computes duty only when dutyCents is undefined. This is latent today, because migrateV1 never sets dutyCents and the v2 payload is rebuilt on every call. It becomes real once v2 is persisted and edited.

findings.title: In-bond (QP/WP) and standalone cargo release (SE) builders have never been sent to CERT
findings.evidence: inbond/builder.ts (829 lines) and cargoRelease/builder.ts (1082 lines) are tested only against the spec. The live SE evidence is the SX derived from AE certification in scenario 061. 061 surfaced SX defects (11022/11119 zero entry value from space-padded numerics) that the AE side had accepted 80+ times (project memory). routes/inbond.ts:215 already builds QP wire for users.
findings.problem: Experience on 061 shows these builders will hit wire-level surprises on first contact with CERT (padding, ordering, which fields ACE derives from). Exposing them to customers as filing-ready risks rejections or wrong in-bond movements, which are bond liabilities.
findings.recommendation: Before any native exposure, run a CERT test pack for SE (types 01/11, add, replace, cancel) and QP/WP (add, arrive, export, delete), arranged with the client rep. Capture the golden wires CBP accepts. Label in-bond as 'not transmitted' in the UI until then.
findings.correction: Verified. The builders are 829 and 1082 lines. routes/inbond.ts POST /:id/build stores wireText and sets status 'READY' for user filings (mounted at /api/v1/inbond). The 'READY' label suggests the filing is ready to transmit.

findings.title: Entries cannot carry AD/CVD cases or entry type 03; AD/CVD goods can only be filed as type 01 with no case and no warning
findings.evidence: schemas/abiDocument.ts:188 `entryType: z.enum(['01', '11', '86'])`. The v1 AbiItem type (services/abi/types.ts:96-118) and abiItemSchema have no AD/CVD case number, deposit rate or bond/cash field. grep for adCvd/antidumping across services/abi, schemas and migrateV1 returns nothing. migrateV1.migrateItem never sets adCvdCases. The native AE stack fully supports them: schemaV2 zAdCvdCaseV2, the engine's 88-record subtotals (engine.ts:203-212, 252-258), and cert scenario 043. Step6Review.tsx:541 renders adCvdCents, but it is always 0 from platform data.
findings.problem: Importers of goods under antidumping or countervailing duty orders must file type 03 and declare the case number and cash deposit. China-origin steel, aluminum extrusions, solar, furniture and many chemicals are common examples. The platform cannot express this at all. A user filing such goods gets a type 01 entry with no AD/CVD declaration, which is evasion-shaped under 19 USC 1592 and EAPA. No warning appears, and the duty estimate shows $0 AD/CVD. The native engine already supports AD/CVD, so the gap is entirely in the platform data model and the migrator, a CC-era limitation.
findings.recommendation: Add entry type 03 and a per-line adCvdCases array (case number, deposit rate or amount, bond/cash code, manufacturer/exporter) to the v1 schema and wizard, and map it in migrateV1. Until then, warn or block when HTS and origin match a known AD/CVD scope: seed the list from Commerce's ACCESS case list or CBP's AD/CVD messages. Show AD/CVD in the estimate.

findings.title: No SPI (preference program) claim is captured or migrated, so native entries cannot claim USMCA or FTA treatment or the MPF exemption
findings.evidence: engine.ts:116-138 and :175 implement SPI pricing and the MPF_EXEMPT_SPI exemption (fees.ts:73-88, cert-proven on F632/F633). However, spiClaimCode appears only in abi-engine files (schemaV2, toAeInput, builder, engine, scenarios), never in services/abi/types.ts, schemas/abiDocument.ts, migrateV1.ts or the abi-wizard components. Only the unrelated schemas/dutyCalculation.ts has an `spi` field.
findings.problem: Every entry built from platform data is priced and transmitted at the column-1 general rate, with full MPF. A USMCA, KORUS or Chile shipment overpays duty and MPF that the importer must recover by PSC or protest. The wizard estimate overstates landed cost for every FTA-eligible line. For a broker product this is a core capability gap. The engine work is already done and cert-proven, but the platform never feeds it.
findings.recommendation: Add a per-line spiClaimCode, validated against AE Table 8 and the HTS special column, to the v1 schema and the wizard, and map it in migrateV1. Combine this with ENG-04's lapsed-program table so GSP claims keep the indicator but deposit at the general rate. Add tests for the MPF exemption from the scenario 054 and 040 shapes.

findings.title: Plain-rate ch.99 headings are priced as add-ons, but ACE treats them as replacing column 1 (F624 on EU/JP/KR/CH/TW lines and 232 'sum' headings)
findings.evidence:
engine.ts:149-152 prices every value-0 '99' tariff on the base value: `tariff.valueDollars === 0 && tariff.htsNumber.startsWith('99') && othersValueDollars > 0 ? othersValueDollars : tariff.valueDollars`. The base tariff is still priced at its own column-1 rate, and nothing zeroes it. engine.ts:144-148 even cites 9903.41.10 '40%' as covered.

Live USITC general-column text (2026-10-15): 9903.05.74 (CH, column 1 < 12.5%) = '12.5%'; 9903.05.39 (EU, column 1 < 10%) = '10%'; 9903.82.10 = '15%'.

CERT ground truth, with duties pinned by hand:
- scenarios/index.ts:854-856: "'[1902194000] replaced' — the NT52 12.5% IS the header's whole duty; the conventional 6.4% is REPLACED, not added"
- index.ts:232-239: Karl's key, "9903.82.10 is 15% 21852.30. 0% on the 1-97 line" (base pinned dutyCents: 0)
- index.ts:1018-1021: 9903.41.10 "IN-LIEU ... (40% + 12.5% + 10% drew F624 live 9/1)"
- index.ts:1367: JP 9903.05.49 "replaced"

Probe of the WIP path: CH $5,000 line gives engine 945.00 vs ACE 625.00; MX $145,682 line with 9903.82.10 gives 25,057.30 vs the CERT-accepted 21,852.30.
findings.problem:
Most goods from the EU, Japan, Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan have a column-1 rate below the NT52 threshold, so they take the plain-rate twin heading. Derivative 232 'sum' headings (.07/.10/.23/.25) and 9903.41.10 behave the same way. On all of these the WIP path deposits column-1 duty on top of the total rate.

Example: an EU line at 3% column 1 on $10,000 is priced at $1,300 instead of $1,000. ACE rejects with F624; if it does not, the importer overpays and the estimate shown to the user is wrong.

The certification scenarios only passed because dutyCents were pinned by hand, so nothing in the engine knows this rule.
findings.recommendation:
Give ch.99 headings explicit semantics, derived from the rate text and overridable per heading in a catalog:
- 'The duty provided in the applicable subheading + X%' = ADDITIONAL: computed on the ch.1-97 value; the base keeps its duty.
- Plain 'X%' = REPLACEMENT / TOP_UP_TOTAL: computed on the base value; the base 50-record deposits 0 (ACE's 'replaced').
- 'The duty provided in the applicable subheading' and 'No change' = NO_ADDITIONAL (see MHT-02).

Pick twins (9903.05.38 vs .39, 9903.82.10 vs .11, .07 vs .08) by comparing column 1's ad valorem equivalent with the threshold. Then remove the pinned dutyCents in scenarios 006, 019, 024 and 036 and assert the computed values as regression tests.
